verifications.claim: The Jones Act is the Merchant Marine Act of 1920.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "the Merchant Marine Act—better known as the Jones Act" (R1); "Under the Merchant Marine Act of 1920, more commonly called the Jones Act" (R2); "The Merchant Marine Act of 1920, commonly known as the Jones Act" (R3, R4); "Section 27 of the Merchant Marine Act is known as the Jones Act" (R5); "Section 27 of the Merchant Marine Act of 1920... referred to as the Jones Act" (R6); "The Jones Act, also known as the Merchant Marine Act of 1920" (R7)
verifications.reasoning: Multiple sources directly identify the Jones Act as the Merchant Marine Act of 1920 or Section 27 thereof.

verifications.claim: The Jones Act is a federal statute.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.reasoning: Sources explicitly describe it as a U.S. federal statute enacted by Congress.

verifications.claim: The Jones Act requires that all goods transported by water between U.S. ports be carried on U.S.-built ships.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "the vessels to have been built or rebuilt in the United States" (R1); "ships that were built in America" (R2); "Be built in the United States" (R3); "built in the United States" (R4); "ships that have been constructed in the United States" (R5); "US-built" (R6); "US-flag ships" implying U.S.-built (R7)
verifications.reasoning: All relevant sources confirm the U.S.-build requirement for vessels in domestic trade.

verifications.claim: The Jones Act requires that all goods transported by water between U.S. ports be carried on U.S.-flagged ships.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "Only qualified ships... between U.S. ports" with U.S. requirements (R1); "U.S.-flagged ships" (R2); "U.S.-flagged vessels" (R3); "flagged (or registered in the United States)" (R4); "fly the U.S. flag" (R5); "U.S. flag ships" (R6)
verifications.reasoning: Sources consistently state U.S. flag requirement for coastwise trade.

verifications.claim: Under the Jones Act, vessels must be at least 75% owned by U.S. citizens.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "at least 75 percent U.S. vessel ownership" (R1); "owned by U.S. citizens or permanent residents" (R3); "owned by a company with 75% U.S. ownership" (R4); "owned by U.S. citizens" (R5); "owned by a US company" (R6); "over 75% of the ownership stake held by U.S. citizens" (R11)
verifications.reasoning: Sources directly specify 75% U.S. ownership requirement.

verifications.claim: Under the Jones Act, vessels must be built in the U.S.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "built or rebuilt in the United States" (R1); "built in America" (R2); "Be built in the United States" (R3); "built in the United States" (R4); "constructed in the United States" (R5); "US-built" (R6); "U.S.-built" (R11)

verifications.claim: Under the Jones Act, vessels must be crewed primarily by U.S. citizens or permanent residents.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "at least 75 percent of the crew to be U.S. citizens or permanent residents" (R1); "crewed by at least 75% American mariners" (R3); "crewed by 75% American sailors" (R4); "crewed by U.S. citizens and U.S. permanent residents" (R5); "crews consisting of American citizens" (R6); "At least 75% of a ship's crew must be U.S. citizens" (R11)

verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "cabotage—the transport of products between ports within a nation’s domestic boundaries" (R1); "Cabotage is the trade between two ports within the same country" (R4); "Cabotage is the transport of goods or passengers between two points in the same country" (R5)
verifications.reasoning: Direct definitions match domestic trade, specifically waterborne in context.

verifications.claim: The Jones Act was enacted to protect the domestic maritime industry and ensure national security.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "protect their national security, support their ship manufacturers" (R1); "protect and sustain the U.S. shipbuilding industry... national defense" (R3); "support the shipbuilding industry... military auxiliary" (R4); "national defense" (R5); "critical to the military strategy... national security" (R6)
verifications.reasoning: Sources state purposes of protecting industry and security.

verifications.claim: The Jones Act applies to all domestic shipping.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "transport cargo between U.S. ports" (R1); "domestic trade" (R3); "coastwise trade" (R4); "movement of cargo between two points in the United States" (R6)
verifications.reasoning: Applies to all coastwise/domestic waterborne shipping between U.S. ports; context implies maritime.

verifications.claim: The Jones Act applies to shipping to non-continental locations like Alaska, Hawaii, and Puerto Rico.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "including those in Hawaii, Alaska, Guam, and Puerto Rico" (R1); "Alaska... Puerto Rico" (R2); "Hawaii, Alaska, and Puerto Rico" (R3); "Puerto Rico, Hawaii, Alaska" (R5)

verifications.claim: Proponents argue the Jones Act is vital for national security by maintaining a U.S. merchant marine and shipyard capacity.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "robust reserve fleet... shipbuilding businesses" (R1); "Enhances National Security... shipbuilding capabilities" (R3); "serve as a military auxiliary... shipbuilding industry" (R4); "maintains its expertise in shipbuilding... sealift needs" (R6)

verifications.claim: Critics argue the Jones Act increases shipping costs.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "higher shipping costs" (R1); "much more difficult—and expensive" (R2); "Increases Shipping Costs for Domestic Trade" (R3); "increases the prices" (R8); "significantly increases shipping costs" (R11)

verifications.claim: Critics argue the Jones Act reduces competition.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "restrictions on foreign competition" (R2); "limits market competition... stifle competition" (R3)
verifications.reasoning: Direct statements from critics on reduced competition.

verifications.claim: Critics argue the Jones Act harms economies in non-contiguous areas.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "higher shipping costs... outside the continental United States" (R1); "Puerto Rico pay more... Hawaii" (R2); "Hawaii, Alaska, and Puerto Rico – Higher costs" (R3); "hinder economic development in Puerto Rico" (R5)
verifications.reasoning: Critics link to economic harm in non-contiguous areas.

verifications.claim: The Jones Act often leads to calls for waivers during emergencies.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "in times of a federally declared emergency... Hurricane Maria" (R1); "waived... Hurricane Maria... Hurricane Fiona" (R2); numerous waiver examples post-hurricanes (R5); "waiving the requirements... natural disasters" (R8)
verifications.reasoning: Sources document frequent waiver requests/calls in emergencies.

verifications.claim: The Jones Act allows U.S. seamen injured at sea to bring personal injury lawsuits against their employers.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "allows injured sailors to make claims... against their employers" (R5); "enables seamen who have been injured at sea... to bring a personal injury action against their employers" (R7)

verifications.claim: The Jones Act was introduced by Senator Wesley Jones.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "Introduced in the Senate by Wesley Jones (R–WA)" (R5); "in honor of its author, Senator Wesley Jones (R-WA)" (R6); "U.S. Senator Wesley Jones of Washington introduced the Act" (R11)

verifications.claim: The Jones Act has been in place for over a century.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "97th anniversary" (2017, R4); "passed the bill 105 years ago" (R9); "since 1920" (R11)
verifications.reasoning: Enacted 1920; sources confirm 100+ years in current context.
